title: Sharp and Adaptive Cluster Recovery in Slowly Mixing Gaussian Hidden Markov Models

paper.title: Sharp and Adaptive Cluster Recovery in Slowly Mixing Gaussian Hidden Markov Models
paper.abstract:
We study cluster recovery in a two-state Gaussian hidden Markov model in the slowly mixing regime, where the transition probability δ \delta may vanish with the sample size. Temporal persistence creates long homogeneous segments and fundamentally changes the recovery problem relative to the i.i.d. Gaussian mixture benchmark. Rather than being purely adverse, label dependence provides exploitable structure: the statistical difficulty becomes concentrated near the rare transition points, giving rise to recovery regimes governed explicitly by their frequency δ \delta . We first characterize, up to universal constants, the oracle Bayes
risk for offline and online clustering. Both problems exhibit a
nonstandard polynomial risk regime, but the sequential constraint
induces an additional logarithmic localization cost, yielding a genuine
online/offline gap. We also study fixed lag prediction with delayed
label feedback and identify the effective memory horizon beyond which
past labels no longer improve the optimal rate. When the signal direction is unknown and possibly high dimensional,
the problem is governed by the effective signal strength r n 2 = ‖ θ ‖ 4 / σ 4 ‖ θ ‖ 2 / σ 2 + d / n . r_{n}^{2}=\frac{\|\theta\|^{4}/\sigma^{4}}{\|\theta\|^{2}/\sigma^{2}+d/n}. We derive minimax lower bounds and construct fully adaptive
polynomial time procedures attaining the sharp recovery rates. In
particular, almost full recovery is possible precisely when r n 2 ≫ δ r_{n}^{2}\gg\delta . If n ​ δ ≳ log ⁡ n n\delta\gtrsim\log n , adaptation to both the
signal θ \theta and the transition probability δ \delta incurs no first order loss, and
the sharp exact recovery threshold (under the Hamming loss) is r n 2 = 2 ​ log ⁡ ( n ​ δ ) ​ ( 1 + o ⁡ ( 1 ) ) . r_{n}^{2}=2\log(n\delta)\,(1+o(1)). Thus the effective complexity of the problem is governed by the number
of latent transitions, rather than by the sample size itself.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Clustering is a fundamental problem in unsupervised learning: given observations generated from a heterogeneous population, the objective is to recover the latent groups without observing their labels. A large body of work has developed algorithms and statistical guarantees for mixture models under an independence assumption; see, among many others, [ 10 , 19 , 16 , 7 , 17 ] , and the surveys in [ 9 , 8 ] . In many applications, however, observations arrive sequentially and the latent states exhibit substantial temporal persistence. Treating such data as i.i.d. can therefore miss an important source of statistical information. We study this phenomenon in a two-state Gaussian hidden Markov model. The observations satisfy X i = η i θ + σ ξ i , i = 1 , … , n , X_{i}=\eta_{i}\theta+\sigma\xi_{i},\qquad i=1,\dots,n, (1) where θ ∈ ℝ d \theta\in\mathbb{R}^{d} is an unknown signal vector, σ > 0 \sigma>0 is the noise standard deviation, ξ i ∼ i . i . d . 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , I d ) \xi_{i}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathrm{i.i.d.}}}{{\sim}}\mathcal{N}(0,I_{d}) , and ( η i ) i ∈ [ n ] (\eta_{i})_{i\in[n]} is a stationary symmetric Markov chain on { − 1 , + 1 } \{-1,+1\} with transition matrix Q = ( 1 − δ δ δ 1 − δ ) , 0 < δ ≤ 1 2 . Q=\begin{pmatrix}1-\delta&\delta\\ \delta&1-\delta\end{pmatrix},\qquad 0<\delta\leq\frac{1}{2}. The parameter δ \delta controls the persistence of the hidden labels. At δ = 1 / 2 \delta=1/2 , the labels are independent and the model reduces to the balanced two-component Gaussian mixture. Our focus is on the slowly mixing regime, in which δ \delta may vanish with n n and is not assumed to be bounded below by a positive constant. The regime δ ≥ 1 / n \delta\geq 1/n . Throughout the paper, we will often restrict attention to δ ≥ 1 n . \delta\geq\frac{1}{n}. This is a natural nondegeneracy condition. The expected number of transitions is ( n − 1 ) ​ δ (n-1)\delta , whereas ℙ ⁡ ( η 1 = ⋯ = η n ) = ( 1 − δ ) n − 1 . \mathbb{P}(\eta_{1}=\cdots=\eta_{n})=(1-\delta)^{n-1}. Hence, if δ ≲ 1 / n \delta\lesssim 1/n , the latent path has no transition with probability bounded away from zero. If δ = o ⁡ ( 1 / n ) \delta=o(1/n) , this probability tends to one. On this event the sample contains a single latent cluster and recovery, modulo the global label permutation, is trivial. The lower bound δ ≥ 1 / n \delta\geq 1/n excludes the asymptotically transition-free regime n ​ δ → 0 n\delta\to 0 , but still permits paths with only a bounded expected number of transitions. The noise level σ \sigma . For simplicity, several constructions below are stated for known σ \sigma , and the oracle analysis is normalized to σ = 1 \sigma=1 . Estimating σ \sigma is orthogonal to the slowly mixing structure: the dependence of the hidden labels affects the low-rank signal component, whereas the isotropic Gaussian noise level can be estimated by standard moment or spectral methods. Thus a consistent estimator of σ \sigma may be plugged into the procedures below without changing the rates or phase transitions. We therefore treat σ \sigma as known and focus on the difficulties created by the latent Markov structure. Slow mixing changes the geometry of the recovery problem. A typical latent trajectory consists of long constant stretches separated by relatively few transition points. As a consequence, clustering is no longer governed solely by the overlap of two Gaussian components. Away from a transition, many neighboring observations carry information about the same hidden state, whereas observations near transition points are the most difficult to assign correctly. This suggests the heuristic decomposition Clustering risk ≈ Transition frequency × Localization error per transition . \text{Clustering risk}\approx\text{Transition frequency}\times\text{Localization error per transition}. This connection with change-point localization is one of the main structural themes of the paper. Related Gaussian change-point problems are studied, for example, in [ 21 ] , but the present setting differs in that both the number and the locations of the changes are random and generated by a Markov chain, and the loss is a global clustering loss modulo label permutation. We first study an oracle problem in which the model parameters are known. This isolates the intrinsic effect of temporal dependence from the difficulty of estimating the signal direction. We consider both offline clustering, in which the full trajectory ( X 1 , … , X n ) (X_{1},\dots,X_{n}) is available before any decision is made, and online clustering, in which assignments are made sequentially and cannot be revised. The two settings exhibit the same weak-signal threshold, but they differ substantially in the intermediate signal regime. Offline access to observations on both sides of a potential transition removes the additional delay cost that appears in the online problem. We also introduce a fixed-lag online prediction problem in which labels are revealed after a fixed lag. This auxiliary model provides a useful benchmark for understanding how much information is carried by recent historical labels and plays a role in the analysis of the online lower bound. We then turn to the statistically more demanding setting in which θ \theta is unknown and may be high-dimensional. For the minimax class Θ ⁡ ( Δ ) = { θ ∈ ℝ d : ‖ θ ‖ ≥ Δ } , \Theta(\Delta)=\{\theta\in\mathbb{R}^{d}:\|\theta\|\geq\Delta\}, the effective signal is r n 2 = Δ 4 / σ 4 Δ 2 / σ 2 + d / n , r_{n}^{2}=\frac{\Delta^{4}/\sigma^{4}}{\Delta^{2}/\sigma^{2}+d/n}, (2) which is the same high-dimensional signal parameter that appears in the i.i.d. two-component Gaussian mixture [ 17 ] . The Markov structure enters through δ \delta : our lower bounds identify r n 2 ≍ δ r_{n}^{2}\asymp\delta as the onset of nontrivial recovery, rather than the constant-order threshold of the i.i.d. model. We complement these lower bounds with adaptive procedures. In particular, we construct estimators of the signal magnitude and an initial label direction, show that δ \delta can be estimated up to a constant factor in the recovery regime, and develop two polynomial-time recovery procedures: an iterative estimator that closely mirrors the oracle construction, and a one-shot sample-splitting estimator that attains the minimax rate. The main contributions can be summarized as follows. 1. We characterize the oracle Bayes risk for offline clustering in a slowly mixing Gaussian HMM and identify the weak, intermediate, and strong-signal regimes. In particular, temporal persistence lowers the threshold for almost full recovery from constant order in the i.i.d. model to the transition scale δ \delta . 2. We characterize the corresponding online Bayes risk. The sequential constraint creates an additional logarithmic localization cost in the intermediate regime, revealing a genuine online/offline gap. 3. We analyze the fixed-lag online prediction problem and identify a critical lag separating a memory-dominated regime, in which a recently revealed label is the most useful source of information, from an observation dominated regime, in which sufficiently old labels no longer improve the optimal rate. 4. In the unknown direction high-dimensional problem, we derive minimax lower bounds and fully adaptive polynomial-time procedures. Almost full recovery occurs exactly when r n 2 ≫ δ r_{n}^{2}\gg\delta and when n ​ δ ≥ C 0 ​ log ⁡ n n\delta\geq C_{0}\log n for a sufficiently large universal constant C 0 C_{0} , the sharp first-order exact-recovery threshold is r n 2 = 2 ​ log ⁡ ( n ​ δ ) ​ ( 1 + o ⁡ ( 1 ) ) r_{n}^{2}=2\log(n\delta)(1+o(1)) . The adaptive ingredients include signal strength estimation, a spectral label initializer, and constant factor estimation of the transition probability δ \delta .

sections.heading: 2 Related literature
sections.text: Our work lies at the intersection of clustering in mixture models, inference in hidden Markov models, and change-point detection and localization. Clustering in Gaussian mixtures. The balanced two-component Gaussian mixture is the natural independent benchmark for label recovery. A broad literature studies computationally efficient procedures and sharp statistical guarantees, including spectral methods [ 10 , 19 ] , Lloyd-type algorithms [ 13 ] , semidefinite relaxations [ 16 , 7 , 18 , 5 ] , and related methods. In particular, [ 17 ] gives a sharp minimax analysis under Hamming loss modulo the global label permutation. For minimax classes satisfying ‖ θ ‖ ≥ Δ \|\theta\|\geq\Delta , the relevant effective signal is r n 2 r_{n}^{2} defined in ( 2 ). The same quantity governs our high-dimensional lower and upper bounds. The essential difference is that the labels are no longer independent: their persistence introduces the additional scale δ \delta and converts much of the recovery problem into localization around random transition times. Inference and decision problems in hidden Markov models. Hidden Markov models provide a canonical framework for inference with dependent latent states; see, for example, [ 3 ] . Classical statistical theory has largely focused on estimation of the model parameters. Consistency and asymptotic normality of likelihood-based estimators were established under suitable ergodicity and forgetting conditions by, among others, [ 2 ] and [ 4 ] . Nonparametric identification and maximum likelihood estimation for finite-state hidden Markov models were studied by [ 1 ] . A related decision-theoretic literature exploits latent Markov dependence for structured inference. For instance, [ 20 ] considers large-scale multiple testing under a two-state hidden Markov model and constructs oracle and asymptotically optimal data-driven procedures that exploit dependence between the latent states. The inferential target there is multiple testing rather than recovery of the entire latent sequence under clustering loss. The closest work to ours is [ 6 ] , which studies clustering in a general nonparametric HMM framework. Their results are tailored to strongly mixing chains, with transition probabilities bounded away from zero. The regime considered here is complementary: δ \delta may vanish with n n , so the usual mixing and forgetting constants are no longer uniform and the dependence on δ \delta becomes part of the statistical difficulty itself. This leads to polynomial-risk regimes and recovery thresholds that disappear when the mixing parameters are treated as fixed constants. Our focus is also different from classical parameter estimation: the primary target is sharp recovery of the latent state sequence. Change-point detection and localization. When δ ≪ 1 \delta\ll 1 , a typical hidden path is piecewise constant with relatively few changes, which creates a close connection with change-point problems. Minimax detection and localization rates for Gaussian sequences have been studied extensively; see, for example, [ 21 ] and the review [ 26 ] . In high dimensions, projection-based reductions and sparse change-point detection are particularly relevant to our setting. In [ 22 ] an informative sparse projection direction is estimated before reducing the problem to univariate change-point estimation, while [ 12 ] characterize the minimax testing rates for detecting a single sparse change in a high-dimensional Gaussian mean vector. Finite-sample guarantees for detection and localization of changes in high-dimensional mean vectors were obtained by [ 25 ] . Change-point segmentation under temporal dependence has also been considered in more general time-series settings; see, for example, [ 28 ] . The analogy with change-point analysis is useful but not exact. In our setting, both the number and the locations of the changes are random and generated by the latent Markov chain; the signal direction may be unknown and high-dimensional; and the loss concerns global recovery of the latent sequence modulo a label permutation rather than detection or localization of a fixed collection of deterministic change-points. In particular, the transition frequency δ \delta plays simultaneously the role of a stochastic change-point intensity and a fundamental scale in the recovery risk. Estimation of the emission parameter. A complementary line of work concerns estimation of θ \theta up to sign. In the Gaussian location model, corresponding to perfectly constant labels, the minimax estimation rate is d / n \sqrt{d/n} ; see [ 24 ] . In the i.i.d. Gaussian mixture model, [ 23 ] establish minimax rates for estimating θ \theta and analyze spectral and EM-type procedures. For Markov-dependent labels, [ 27 ] study estimation over a range of transition probabilities and show that temporal dependence can improve estimation. A spectral procedure from that work was revisited in [ 11 ] , where an adaptive bucketed spectral estimator was developed. These estimation results provide useful ingredients for our adaptive clustering procedures, but the statistical target here is different: the oracle part of the paper isolates the intrinsic label-recovery difficulty, while the minimax part quantifies the additional cost of learning an unknown high-dimensional signal direction.

sections.heading: 4 Main results
sections.text: We begin with the oracle problem, in which the signal vector and the transition probability are known. The delayed-label model is analyzed first because it isolates the value of recent label information and provides a useful benchmark for the online lower bound. We then compare online and offline clustering. The final part of the section removes oracle knowledge and develops adaptive high-dimensional procedures. Throughout the oracle analysis, we normalize the noise level to σ = 1 \sigma=1 . Temporal persistence creates long homogeneous segments and fundamentally changes the recovery problem relative to the i.i.d. Gaussian mixture benchmark. Rather than being purely adverse, label dependence provides exploitable structure: the statistical difficulty becomes concentrated near the rare transition points, giving rise to recovery regimes governed explicitly by their frequency δ \delta . We first characterize, up to universal constants, the oracle Bayes risk for offline and online clustering. Both problems exhibit a nonstandard polynomial risk regime, but the sequential constraint induces an additional logarithmic localization cost, yielding a genuine online/offline gap. We also study fixed lag prediction with delayed label feedback and identify the effective memory horizon beyond which past labels no longer improve the optimal rate. When the signal direction is unknown and possibly high dimensional, the problem is governed by the effective signal strength r n 2 = ‖ θ ‖ 4 / σ 4 ‖ θ ‖ 2 / σ 2 + d / n . r_{n}^{2}=\frac{\|\theta\|^{4}/\sigma^{4}}{\|\theta\|^{2}/\sigma^{2}+d/n}. We derive minimax lower bounds and construct fully adaptive polynomial time procedures attaining the sharp recovery rates.
